questions.q: When should you use an object instead of an array?
questions.explain: Use an array for a list of similar things in order. Use an object for one thing whose parts have names.
options: When you have a list of similar things in order
When you have one thing with named parts, like a user with a name and an e-mail
When the values are all numbers
Never; arrays can do everything objects can

questions.q: In { name: "Ada", age: 36 }, what is name: "Ada"?
questions.explain: Each piece of an object is a property: a name (the key), a colon, and a value. The value can be anything, even an array or another object.
options: A property: a key, a colon and a value

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A property whose value is a function is a method. Inside it, this is the object the method was called on, here user.

questions.q: What is a method?
questions.explain: A method is a function stored as a property. You call it with parentheses, like user.greet(). A property holding another object makes a nested object.
options: A property whose value is a function
A property whose value is another object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The chain is read left to right: user, then its address, then city. zip does not exist on address, so it is undefined; that is not an error.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'zip')

questions.q: A user has no address property. What happens with user.address.city?
questions.explain: Reading a missing property gives undefined, but reading a property of undefined crashes: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'city').
options: It throws a TypeError, because it reads a property of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Square brackets take a string or a variable: user[field] reads age. user.field looks for a property literally called field, which does not exist.

questions.q: When do you need square brackets, like user[key], instead of a dot?
questions.explain: Use the dot when you know the name while writing the code. Use brackets when the name comes from a variable or contains characters like -.
options: When the property name is stored in a variable, or is not a valid variable name (for example it has a dash)
Only when the property does not exist yet

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: in asks "does this object have a property with this name?". phone exists (with the value undefined); email does not. Reading either one gives undefined.
questions.code:
const user = { name: "Ada", phone: undefined };
console.log("phone" in user, "email" in user, user.phone === user.email);

questions.q: You write user.nmae by mistake. What happens?
questions.explain: Reading a property that does not exist gives undefined. That is convenient, but it is also how typos slip through silently.
options: JavaScript throws "property nmae does not exist"
You get undefined, with no error, so the typo can slip through

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Assigning changes or adds a property, and delete removes it completely. const only stops user from pointing at a different object.

questions.q: You want an object that nobody can change. What does the lesson use?
questions.explain: const does not freeze the object; it only stops the name from pointing elsewhere. Object.freeze stops changes to the object's properties.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A variable holds a reference, an arrow to the object. sameUser = user copies the arrow, not the object, so both names point at the same object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: === on objects asks "is this the same object?", not "do they look the same?". a and b are two separate objects; c points at a.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A function receives the reference, so changing person changes the caller's object. Many backend bugs come from a function quietly changing an object someone else is still using.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A computed property puts an expression in square brackets; its value becomes the property name when the code runs.

questions.q: You want to keep only the text settings of an object. Which approach does the lesson teach?
questions.explain: An object has no map or filter. Turn it into pairs, use the array tools, and turn the pairs back into an object.
options: Object.entries, then an array method like filter, then Object.fromEntries
Use delete inside a for...of loop over the object

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: filter keeps the pairs whose value is a string, and Object.fromEntries turns the pairs back into an object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When two objects have the same property, the one that comes later wins. Put defaults first and the user's choices after them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Object.assign writes into its first argument. Passing a fresh {} keeps defaults untouched; passing defaults itself changes it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Spread makes a shallow copy: name is copied, but address is still the same shared object. Changing the copy's city changes the original's.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: structuredClone makes a deep copy: every level is new, so each user has their own alerts object.

questions.q: An object contains another object. Which statement is true?
questions.explain: Spread is a shallow copy: nested objects stay shared. structuredClone is a deep copy. copy = obj is not a copy at all, just a second name.
options: { ...obj } copies only the top level; structuredClone(obj) copies every level
const copy = obj makes a deep copy

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: ...rest collects every property you did not name into a new object. The original user is not changed; it still has all 3 properties.

questions.q: Your API must return a user without its passwordHash. Which approach is right?
questions.explain: Take the secret field out and send the rest. Never trust the client to ignore data it receives. JSON.stringify does not know which fields are secret, and blanking the stored user would destroy the real hash.
options: Send the whole user; the client will ignore the hash
Set user.passwordHash = "" on the stored user and send it

questions.q: What should a real app store for a user's password?
questions.explain: A real app stores a hash made by a password-hashing library, never the password. The authentication lesson later in the course shows how.
options: The password itself, so it can be shown on a "forgot password" page
A password hash made by a library, never the password itself
The password in JSON, because JSON is safe
The password with its letters reversed

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON.stringify turns a value into JSON text, with double quotes and no spaces. JSON.parse turns the text back into a value.
options:
{ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false, tags: [ 'home' ] }
object home

questions.q: Which of these is valid JSON?
questions.explain: In JSON, property names and strings must use double quotes, and there are no comments and no trailing commas.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: JSON only knows strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. undefined and methods vanish, and the date becomes a string that stays a string after JSON.parse.

questions.q: Your API receives JSON with a due date. After JSON.parse, what do you have?
questions.explain: JSON is text, and JSON.parse only builds plain data. Dates arrive as strings. Always check and convert incoming data yourself.
options: Plain data: due is a string, and you must check and convert it yourself
A function that returns the date
An error, because JSON cannot contain dates

questions.q: What does the null, 2 in JSON.stringify(task, null, 2) do?
questions.explain: The third argument sets the indentation. The output is the same data, spread over several lines.
options: It removes null values and keeps 2 properties
It indents the JSON with two spaces, which is easier to read
It limits the output to 2 levels deep

questions.q: A user only asked to change their theme. What does this print?
questions.explain: Spreading everything the client sent copied role too, and made the user an administrator. This security bug is called mass assignment.

questions.q: How do you fix the mass assignment bug in updateProfile?
questions.explain: An allow-list names exactly which fields are accepted. Removing only role (a block-list) fails as soon as another sensitive field like id is sent. Spreading the profile second would stop all changes, including the allowed ones.
options: Spread the changes first and the profile second
Use an allow-list of the fields a user may change, and ignore every other field
Delete role from the changes, and allow everything else
Check that the JSON text is shorter than 100 characters

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Only keys on the allow-list get through, so id and role are ignored. The function returns a new object and never changes its input, so ada.bio is still empty.

questions.q: In the profile system, who decides a new profile's role?
questions.explain: createProfile sets role: "user" itself and ignores any role in the input. Anything about permissions must come from the server.
options: The user, through the sign-up form
The server; the role is always set by the server, never taken from user input
Whoever sends the most recent JSON
The client app, before it sends the JSON

questions.q: Finish filledFields(profile) with Object.values: return how many properties have a value that is not an empty string. The program should print 2 0.
questions.explain: Object.values gives an array of the values, so you can use filter and length on it.

questions.q: Finish withPrefix(obj, prefix): return a new object where every key starts with prefix. Use Object.entries, map and Object.fromEntries, and do not change obj.
questions.explain: Turn the object into pairs, change each key with map, and turn the pairs back into an object.

questions.q: Finish updateProfile(profile, changes) safely. Only keys listed in EDITABLE may change; ignore every other key. Return a new object and do not change profile.
questions.explain: Filter the incoming pairs with the allow-list, then spread only the allowed ones over a copy of the profile. role and id never get through.

questions.q: Finish toPublic(profile): use destructuring with ...rest to drop role and passwordHash, and add isAdmin (true when the role is "admin"). The program prints the result as JSON.
questions.explain: Name the fields you must not send; ...rest collects everything else. Then build the public object from rest plus the computed field.

questions.q: Changing Grace's alerts must not change Ada's. Finish newUser(name) so each user gets their own deep copy of defaultSettings. The program should print true false true.
questions.explain: { ...defaultSettings } would copy only one level, so all users would share one alerts object. structuredClone copies every level.

questions.q: Finish buildSettings(chosen) with spread: start from DEFAULTS and let the values in chosen win. Do not change DEFAULTS.
questions.explain: The object spread later wins, so put DEFAULTS first and chosen second. Spread builds a new object, so DEFAULTS stays as it was.

questions.q: Finish parseTask(text): parse the JSON text and return a line TITLE (done) or TITLE (open), depending on the done property.
questions.explain: JSON.parse turns the text back into an object, so you can read task.title and task.done.

questions.q: Finish countByStatus(tasks): return an object that counts how many tasks have each status. Use square brackets to read and write the count for each status.
questions.explain: The property name is in a variable, so use brackets: counts[task.status]. A missing property is undefined, so start it at 0 with ?? 0.

questions.q: With const name = "Ada";, what does { name } mean?
questions.explain: That is shorthand: when the property name and the variable name are the same, you write the name once.
options: { name: name }, an object with a name property whose value is "Ada"
An object with one property called 0

questions.q: What does a variable like const user = { name: "Ada" }; actually hold?
questions.explain: Variables hold references to objects. Assigning the object to another variable copies the arrow, so both names point at the same object.
options: A full copy of the object, so every variable has its own
A reference: an arrow pointing at the object
The object turned into JSON text
Only the first property of the object

questions.q: A client sends text that is not valid JSON, and your code calls JSON.parse on it. What happens?
questions.explain: JSON.parse throws a SyntaxError on invalid text. Input from outside can be anything, so a backend must be ready for that; the lesson on errors shows how.
options: It throws an error, which your code must handle
It fixes the text and parses it

questions.q: Finish getField(user, field). The property name is in the variable field. Return "missing" when the object has no such property (use the in operator), otherwise return its value.
questions.explain: The name is in a variable, so read it with square brackets: user[field]. field in user asks whether the property exists. Note the brackets in !(field in user).

questions.q: Add a method describe() to the task object. It returns TITLE [done] or TITLE [open], reading the object's own properties with this.
questions.explain: describe() { … } is the short way to write a method. Inside it, this is the object it was called on, so it sees the new value of done.

questions.q: Finish setting(key, value) with a computed property: return an object whose property name is the value of key. The program should print { theme: 'dark' } { pageSize: 50 }.
questions.explain: Square brackets around the name, { [key]: value }, use the value of key as the property name. Without them, the property would be called key.
